questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C.
Conclusions: I. Some A are C is a possibility. II. All C are B is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The A–B overlap may extend into C, so I is possible. C may also lie wholly inside B while still overlapping B as stated, so II is possible.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some A are B; some B are C.
Conclusions: I. Some A can be C. II. All C are A is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The two stated overlaps can be arranged so A and C overlap, making I possible. They can also be arranged with C wholly inside A while retaining the required B–C and A–B overlaps, making II possible.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; no B is C.
Conclusions: I. All B are C is a possibility. II. Some A may be C.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The first conclusion conflicts with the given separation between B and C. Since A is contained in B, A also cannot overlap C, so the second possibility is impossible. Neither conclusion follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; all B are C.
Conclusions: I. All C are A is a possibility. II. No B is C is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The sets may all coincide, so I is possible. Since B is contained in C, B and C cannot be disjoint in a nonempty syllogism class, so II is not possible.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No A is B; all B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. No A is C is a possibility. II. No B is D is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: A may be kept disjoint from C, satisfying I. The required C–D overlap may be placed in the part of C outside B, so B and D may also be disjoint, satisfying II.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some A are B; no B is C; all D are C.
Conclusions: I. No B can be D. II. All A are C is a possibility. III. All C may be A.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: Because D is contained in C and B is disjoint from C, I follows. The known A–B member cannot be in C, so II is impossible. C may be contained in A without violating the other statements, so III is possible; only III follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No A is B; some B are C; all C are D.
Conclusions: I. Some A are C is a possibility. II. All D are A is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: A may overlap C outside B, so I is possible. The stated B–C member belongs to D and cannot belong to A because A and B are disjoint; therefore D cannot be wholly inside A.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some A are B; some B are C; all C are D.
Conclusions: I. No A is D is a possibility. II. Some D can be B.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The A–B and B–C witnesses need not be the same, so A can be disjoint from D while the premises remain true. The B–C witness is also in D, so some B is D. Both conclusions follow. The slide’s answer marking appears inconsistent with conclusion II; the key here is based on the statements.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No A is B; some B are C.
Conclusions: I. All C are A is a possibility. II. No A is C is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The existing B–C member prevents C from being wholly inside A, because A and B are disjoint. A can be placed disjoint from C, so II is possible and only II follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; no C is D.
Conclusions: I. No A is D is a possibility. II. No A is C is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: Neither statement forces A to overlap D or C. A may be placed disjoint from D, and it may be placed disjoint from C while the required B–C overlap lies outside A. Both possibilities hold.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; all C are D; no D is E.
Conclusions: I. Some A can be C. II. Some B may be E. III. All A are E is a possibility. IV. Some C can be E. V. All E are B is a possibility. VI. All B are E is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.A: Only conclusions I and IV follow
options.C: Only conclusions I, II and III follow
options.D: Only conclusions I, II, III and V follow

questions.explanation: I is possible by placing A within the B–C overlap. II is possible by placing some other B outside C in E. III is possible by placing A in E outside D. IV is impossible because C is within D and D is disjoint from E. V is possible by placing E within B. VI is impossible because the required B–C member is in D, hence outside E.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are not C.
Conclusions: I. Some A cannot be B. II. Some B cannot be C.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: I contradicts All A are B. The second premise directly establishes that some B are outside C, so II follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some A are B; no B is C.
Conclusions: I. Some C cannot be A. II. Some A cannot be C.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The premises do not guarantee that any C exists, so I does not follow. The stated A–B member is outside C because B and C are disjoint, establishing II.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some A are B; no B is C.
Conclusions: I. Some B cannot be A. II. Some B cannot be C.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
options.D: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
options.E: Both conclusion I and conclusion II follow

questions.explanation: The overlap of A and B does not establish that any B lies outside A, so I does not follow. The known A–B member is a B, and no B is C; therefore some B is necessarily outside C, so II follows.
